summary:
Ikaros is a browser-based 3D game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design, launch and fly two missions: docking a cargo shuttle with the International Space Station, and Ikaros, a solar encounter based on the Solar Probe+ power-system design (Landis et al., AIAA 2008-5712).

Every choice has a real cost. In the hangar, mass, budget and power trade against each other; in flight, the physics engine applies Hohmann transfers, the Tsiolkovsky equation, Kepler orbits and the paper's thermal equations, so players feel why missions use Venus flybys or why solar arrays must retract near the Sun. Technologies beyond today's state of the art are clearly marked as theoretical, and every number in the game cites its source.

Atlas, a holographic mission controller, narrates a prologue, explains what to do and shares real facts in English or Spanish. A post-mission report compares the player's results with real missions such as Hubble servicing and Parker Solar Probe. Ikaros turns mission design into play, helping students understand the trade-offs NASA engineers face every day.
details:
What it does: Ikaros is a browser-based 3D game where players design, launch and fly two missions using real physics:

  • Docking with the ISS: load a Space Shuttle, catch the station with a Hohmann transfer, then pilot the final 122 m approach manually, as real crews did.
  • Ikaros: a solar encounter built on the NASA/JHU-APL paper “Solar Power System Design for the Solar Probe+ Mission” (Landis et al., AIAA 2008-5712). Players must manage the paper’s real limits: 510 times Earth’s sunlight at 9.5 solar radii, solar arrays that fold or tilt to survive, cells kept near 120 °C and at least 482 W of power.

The record: Parker Solar Probe holds the real closest-approach record, at 9.86 solar radii (6.1 million km from the surface, December 2024). With a theoretical kit (mini reactor, superconducting magnetic shield and repair nanobots), players attempt a dive to 850,000 km from the Sun’s center, about eight times closer. Every speculative technology is clearly marked ⚗.

Atlas: a bilingual (English/Spanish) holographic mission controller who narrates, guides each step and shares sourced facts, with a voice cloned locally from a team member, with her consent.

Benefits and impact: players learn orbital mechanics and spacecraft design by making trade-offs and seeing the consequences. Every number cites its source, and the final report compares results with real missions. Our goal is to make mission design accessible, especially to Spanish-speaking students.

Tools: TypeScript, React, three.js and React Three Fiber, GLSL shaders, the Web Audio API, Vite, Vitest and GitHub Actions; NASA 3D Resources models; Chatterbox TTS and FFmpeg. AI tools assisted with image generation, voice and coding.

Creativity: a real engineering paper turned into gameplay, a labeled “what if” that goes past a real record, and hands-on mini-games for each mission phase.

Factors considered: scientific honesty (real versus theoretical), fidelity versus playability, accessibility (bilingual, keyboard, reduced motion), performance on modest hardware, NASA media guidelines and voice consent.e
